title: Assignment: matrices, frequency, pointers and dynamic arrays
overview: These are Shammunul's answers to the assignment that follows the 2D-array and pointer modules. Each problem reuses one recent tool: a frequency array for counting, a matrix check with a flag, a pointer for a simple calculation, and `realloc` to grow an array one element at a time.

concepts.explain: Update `freq[value]++` as soon as you read each value. Then every later question is a single lookup.
First count every value. Then, on a second pass, count the elements whose frequency is 1.
Diagonal cells (`i == j`) must be 1 and every other cell must be 0. Keep the answer in a flag.
Subtract, then flip the sign if the result is negative. `abs(a - b)` from `<stdlib.h>` does the same.
Start with room for 1 element. Before storing element `i`, resize the block to `i + 1` elements.

files.title: Absolute difference using pointers
files.what: Reads `A` and `B` through pointers, subtracts, and makes the result positive.
steps: Read `A` and `B`, then point `ptr1` at `A` and `ptr2` at `B`.

files.title: Count occurrences in a matrix
files.what: Builds a frequency array while reading the matrix, then answers each query with `freq[x]`.
steps: Read the matrix, and add 1 to `freq[Numbers[i][j]]` for each cell.
files.complexity: Time O(N·M + X) · Space O(max value)
files.input_note: The sample: a 2×3 matrix, then 3 query numbers.
files.output_note: `2`, `1` and `0` (2 appears twice, 6 once and 7 never), which matches the expected answer.
files.watch_out: The queries are stored starting at index 1. That works because the array has spare room (`X + 5`), but storing from index 0 is less error-prone.

check.q: Why is `freq` sized 100005 when values are at most 1000?
check.a: It's just a safe upper bound. 1001 slots would be enough.

files.title: Count numbers that appear only once
files.what: Counts every value, then counts the elements whose frequency is exactly 1.
steps: Second pass: add 1 to `count` for each element whose `freq` is 1.
files.output_note: `3`: the values 1, 5 and 6 appear once each.
files.watch_out: The second loop goes over the elements. That is only correct because a value with frequency 1 appears once in the array, so it is counted once.

files.title: Is it a unit matrix?
files.what: Checks that the diagonal cells are 1 and all other cells are 0, using a flag.
steps: For each cell: if `i == j`, it must be 1. Otherwise it must be 0. On a mismatch, set `flag = 0` and break out of the inner loop.
files.input_note: A 3×3 matrix with one stray 2 off the diagonal.

check.q: Is a 1×1 matrix `[1]` a unit matrix?
check.a: Yes, so the program prints YES.

files.title: Grow an array one element at a time
files.what: Starts with a 1-element block and uses `realloc` to make room for each new number before storing it.
steps: For each `i`: read the number into `num_array[i]`.
Call `realloc(arr, (i + 1) * sizeof(int))` so there is room for `i + 1` values, then store `arr[i]`.
files.complexity: Time O(N) on average (each `realloc` may copy) · Space O(N)
files.watch_out: `num_array` is an extra fixed-size array that isn't needed. Read into a plain `int x`. Also check whether `realloc` returned `NULL`.

check.q: On the first iteration (i = 0), how big does `realloc` make the block?
check.a: 1 int, the same size as before.

recap: Build a frequency array once, then answer many count questions instantly.
Unit matrix: 1 on the diagonal and 0 everywhere else. Use a flag to check it.
`realloc` lets an array grow as input arrives.
Absolute difference: subtract, then flip the sign if the result is negative.

check_yourself.q: How would you find the value that appears most often, using a frequency array?
check_yourself.a: Count everything, then scan `freq` and keep track of the index with the largest count.

check_yourself.q: Why is it a bad idea to write `arr = realloc(arr, ...)` without checking the result?
check_yourself.a: If `realloc` fails, it returns NULL. That overwrites your only pointer to the old block, so the memory is lost.
